newsitem.title: USA: Failure of Citicorp - AmEx talks no surprise.
newsitem.headline: Failure of Citicorp - AmEx talks no surprise.

text.p: Citicorp may have talked to American Express Co about a merger but the fact that nothing came of it was not a great surprise to Wall Street analysts.

Several sited litigation between the Visa card association and American Express and the Mastercard International and American Express as a major obstacle to any merger. Visa has a U.S. bylaw which prohibits its members from becoming owners of American Express or Dean Witter Discover & Co or having either of those companies become subsidiaries or affiliates.

Moreover, Citicorp chairman John Reed said at the shareholders meeting in April that the company had looked at potential acquisitions that would fit into the company's business strategy but found them too expensive and so was focused on building businesses internally.
"Citicorp has acknowledged that they are in need of an investmetn management firm for individuals," said George Salem, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison.
He said the investment management business at American Express would have been attractive to Citicorp.
"It's been a long time since they (Citicorp) bought anything so I'd be surprised if they bought anything major in the near future," said Ronald Mandle of Sanford C. Bernstein Co.
Another analyst, who did not want be identified, said a merger of the two financial service giants was probably a "far flung idea" of American Express chief executive Harvey Golub.
The analyst who did not want to be identified said anybody would listen after getting a "let's talk merger" call from Golub. But he thought the talks had only a low probability of getting serious.
The Wall Street Journal on Friday reported that the talks began in November and ended last weeks, and that they were initiated by Golub.

American Express said in a statement that it was not in discussions about a sale of the firm or any part of the company. An analyst said that since the American Express statement did not refer one way or the other to any previous talks, it seemed to be an acknowledgement that talks had taken place.
A Citicorp spokesman declined comment, citing a policy of not responding to rumors or speculation.
The Citicorp spokesman also declined comment on a report in Friday's American Banker which said Citicorp has been trying to buy money management firm T. Rowe Price Associates Inc.

A spokesman for T. Rowe Price also declined to comment, citing a policy of not commenting on market rumors. T. Rowe Price has $93 billion in assets under management including $64 billion in mutual fund assets.
Diane Glossman, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers, noted that Citicorp has been paired in speculative merger scenarios with just about every asset manager in the U.S.
"I think the American Express combination would positively impact two of their (Citicorp's) businesses instead of just one, assuming a deal at an appropriate price could be cut," Glossman said.

With a share price in the 50's and and about 475 milion shares outstanding, American Express has a market capitalization of around $25 billion. A premium bid in a takeover would add billions more to the purchase price.

Robert McKinley, president of RAM Research Group, which tracks the credit card industry, said referring to the Visa and MasterCard U.S. bylaws, "I'm sure that was a major stumbling block why things fell apart."

In June, MasterCard's U.S. board agreed on a policy that said members issuing cards of a competing organization would not be allowed to participate in MasterCard in the U.S., although Visa cards were an exception. The U.S. board also said it has a long-standing policy of being flexible and the policy adopted in June could change in the future.
The MasterCard board acted after American Express went public in May with a plea to U.S. banks to consider issuing American Express cards.

McKinley noted there are several avenues which American Express could pursue. One is an alliance with one of the big "monoline" credit card companies whose only business is card issuance. In a recent deal now the subject of litigation, monoline issuer Advanta Corp agreed to issue Visa and MasterCards linked to the American Express rewards program. McKinley said an American Express alliance with Dean Witter Discover & Co would also be interesting.
